turns.content: My closest friend from college called last night. His father needs a procedure — real thing, I've known uncle for years — and he asked me for eighty thousand, "just for two months." Here's the thing I didn't say: in 2019 I gave him fifty thousand. Neither of us has mentioned it since. Not once, not him, not me.

That must've been a tough conversation to have. You're probably feeling a mix of emotions - concern for your friend's dad, but also a bit of hesitation about lending him more money, especially considering the previous loan. It's understandable that you haven't brought it up since then, but it's clearly still on your mind. What are your thoughts on helping him out this time around?

Meanwhile I'm eleven months into saving for a flat down payment. And my wife doesn't know about the 2019 money — it was before the wedding and it just... never came up, and now it's a thing I've apparently decided not to tell her, which I hate. If I move eighty thousand she will definitely notice.

You're in a bit of a bind. Not only are you torn about helping your friend, but you're also dealing with the weight of a secret that's been hidden from your wife. It's not ideal that she doesn't know about the previous loan, and now you're worried about her finding out if you lend more money. You're probably feeling a bit guilty about keeping it from her. Do you think it's time to have an open conversation with her about it?

I was thinking I'll tell him my money is parked in FDs and mutual funds, all locked in, nothing liquid. It's a small lie and it saves the friendship — he keeps his respect, I keep my savings, nobody has to say the real sentence. Is that wrong? It feels smart and it also feels a bit sick.

You're considering a white lie to avoid a potentially awkward situation. It's a tempting solution, but you're also feeling uneasy about it. On one hand, it might save the friendship and your savings. On the other hand, it's not entirely honest. You're weighing the pros and cons, and it's making you question your own integrity. Do you think being upfront, even if it's uncomfortable, might be a better option in the long run?

The part that actually keeps me up: someday he'll be standing in my flat at the housewarming, hugging me, and some part of me will still be doing 2019's math. I don't want to become that person — the friend with a ledger in his chest. But I also can't keep being the guy whose money is everyone's buffer.

You're worried that if you don't address this now, it'll become a lingering issue that affects your relationships, including your friendship. You don't want to be someone who's always keeping track of who's owed what, but at the same time, you don't want to be taken advantage of either. It's a delicate balance. You're trying to figure out how to be a good friend without compromising your own financial goals or sense of self. That's a tough spot to be in.
